rv.q: It’s in the intimate, bittersweet scenes between those two that “Breakfast at Tiffany’s” is best.
The show is pleasant enough, but it's also oddly bloodless, lacking the sharp wit and emotional complexity that made Capote's novella so memorable.
Clarke is affected but not affecting, and a Breakfast without a fetching Holly isn’t much of a meal.

The palette for this show is dark and brooding, closer to something one might associate with Arthur Miller's "A View From the Bridge" than a vista of a gorgeous girl with an empty bookcase but a party always beginning in her head.
What we get instead is a show that feels both overproduced and undercooked, a mixture of scenic spectacle and narrative muddle that never decides what it wants to be when it grows up.
The many scenes stubbornly refuse to add up to much and it remains as flat as Golightly is supposed to be effervescent.
Ultimately, this translation is an inert substitute for both the written and filmed versions, its central characters distant and lacking in warmth.
Maybe it should have played Holly.
But when a girl named Golightly has to work at effervescence, something’s wrong — and it’s wrong throughout the production.

Richard Greenberg's new stage adaptation of Breakfast at Tiffany's is a meandering misfire lacking the charm and oomph of either Capote's 1958 novella or the 1961 movie that cemented Audrey Hepburn's reputation as the height of sophisticated urbanity.
Capote’s wispy memory tale, told principally in carefully carved prose, may be hypnotic on the page, but it’s dull onstage, with too much narration and not enough drama.

Yet her performance, while highly competent, is strangely unmoving; only in a short scene where she sings on her fire escape -- not Moon River, but a melancholy traditional folk tune -- does she truly capture the vulnerability underlying Holly's cultivated coolness.
But Sean Mathias’s underpopulated and somewhat epicene staging drains the life from the story.
Richard Greenberg's adaptation of Truman Capote's classic novella Breakfast at Tiffany's turns out to be earnest, talky, and rather lifeless despite its good intentions.
...there is very little excitement to be found in this drab and dragging stage adaptation, which was penned by Richard Greenberg ("Take Me Out") and is directed by Sean Mathias...
While it’s an interesting approach, and certainly an unexpected one, the story stumbles at finding its grounding in time and place.

cn.t: Critics find this adaptation overly faithful yet dramatically inert, with excessive narration drowning out theatrical vitality. Clarke struggles in Hepburn's shadow as the production fails to capture the novella's charm or emotional depth.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
